nameStory: The "amber jelly" name perfectly captures this fungus's appearance - it looks exactly like a blob of golden amber-colored jelly that someone dropped on a tree branch. The scientific name "recisa" means "cut back" or "trimmed," possibly referring to how these fungi appear to be neatly cut or shaped where they attach to branches.
description: Amber jelly fungus is a small, gelatinous fungus that looks like translucent orange-brown jelly blobs growing on dead branches. These wobbly, top-shaped mushrooms have no cap, stem, or gills - just a smooth, rubbery mass that jiggles when touched. They typically measure just an inch or two across and have a distinctive spinning-top or turban shape. This saprophytic fungus feeds on dead wood, slowly decomposing the branches where it grows.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Completely gelatinous and wobbly - feels like firm jello or rubber when poked, bouncing back to shape when pressed

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Turbinate (top-shaped) with a narrow base that widens toward the top, like an upside-down spinning top or small turban

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Translucent orange-brown to amber, often with a slight golden glow when backlit by sunlight

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on dead but still-attached willow twigs and small branches, rarely on other wood types

idTips.label: Surface
idTips.description: Completely smooth with no gills, pores, or other structures - just a continuous jelly-like surface that may feel slightly sticky

habitat: Look for amber jelly fungus on dead willow branches in wet areas throughout New England - along streams, pond edges, wetlands, and anywhere willows grow. It prefers the smaller dead twigs and branches that are still attached to living willow trees rather than fallen logs. You'll often find multiple specimens clustered together on the same branch system.

seasonality.spring: Fresh fruiting bodies begin appearing as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture. Look for bright, translucent specimens that are plump and jiggly.
seasonality.summer: Active fruiting continues through summer, especially after rainstorms. Hot, dry periods may cause specimens to shrivel and darken temporarily.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for finding specimens as autumn moisture returns. Many remain visible and identifiable even as they begin to dry out and darken.
seasonality.winter: Old fruiting bodies may persist as dark, shriveled masses on branches, but become hard to identify. New growth is minimal in cold weather.

funFact: When amber jelly fungus dries out during hot weather, it shrivels into a hard, dark crust that looks completely dead - but add some rain and it magically plumps back up into its original jelly-blob form within hours, good as new!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other jelly fungi in the same genus, but amber jelly's exclusive preference for willow branches is a dead giveaway. Other jelly fungi grow on different trees - birch jelly prefers birch, pine jelly likes conifers. Remember: "Willow and amber go together."
contextualKnowledge: This species has long been confused with the very similar American Amber Jelly Fungus (Exidia crenata) found in North America, and many field guides may not distinguish between them. Recent research suggests they are distinct species, with true Exidia recisa possibly being a European species that may or may not occur in New England.
compareHints: Amber jelly differs from its relatives mainly by substrate preference - while Black Witches' Butter grows on various hardwoods and appears darker, and birch jelly sticks to birch trees, amber jelly is the willow specialist. American Amber Jelly Fungus is virtually identical but may have slightly different microscopic features and a broader range of host trees.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American Amber Jelly differs from its close relative Black Witches' Butter by staying consistently amber to orange-brown rather than turning black with age.
Black Witches' Butter stands out from its Exidia relatives by its distinctly warty, blister-like surface texture and preference for oak wood.
